title: How many socks to grab in the dark for a pair
description:
In the dark, with 10 black and 10 white socks, 3 socks always give you a matching pair: 2 can be one of each, but the third has only two colors to be. A black pair is different: in the worst case all 10 white socks come out first, so you need 12. It's the pigeonhole principle, and the same argument proves at least 10 Londoners have exactly the same number of hairs (nobody has a million hairs, and London has over 9 million people).

Numbers checked in code: exhaustive worst case over every possible handful, plus 100,000 simulated dark mornings. Sources: Wikipedia, Pigeonhole principle (sock and hair examples) and London (population 9,122,909, 2025).

beats.say: 3 socks for any pair, 12 for a black one.
Not luck. Both numbers are guarantees, even on your worst morning.
Your drawer: 10 black socks, 10 white. Lights off. You can't see a thing.
Grab 2. Worst case: one of each. No pair yet.
Grab a third. It only has two colors to be, so it matches one. Pair.
But today you need black. Now the drawer fights back.
Worst case, all 10 white come out first. 10 grabs, zero black. The next 2 have to be black. 12.
Any pair costs the colors plus one. A chosen color costs every other sock, plus two.
Same trick: nobody has a million hairs, and London has over 9 million people. So at least 10 Londoners share an exact hair count.
